overview: Farmers stay mostly **calm** under AI Plateau and AGI by 2036, and **keep going**, worrying more about prices, rent and farm sales.
**AGI by 2028** is the shock: worry jumps to 3.4 out of 5, and most **save, cut spending** and lean on family.
In every scenario, **savings** and **adaptability** decide who stays calm; farmers who resist change and have thin savings worry most.

S0.headline: Most farmers carry on as before and treat AI as a small helper, while money, prices and the farm's owners stay their real worries.

whatTheyDo.text: About 85% keep farming exactly as now, such as doing the morning and evening feeds or finishing the same number of pigs a year.
About 41% put more aside, for example fifty pounds a month or £150 a month towards a stake in the farm.
About 37% keep using AI where it helps, such as a feed planner, shop orders or growing a veg box scheme.
About 21% look for extra money on the side, like weekend loading shifts or selling beef boxes online.
About 18% cut back, for example buying own-brand food or skipping the summer holiday.

whatTheySay: Most say **"I told you so"**: the AI talk was hype and cows still need milking at five.
They say good farming is done with **eyes and hands**, and AI belongs in the office.
whatTheyThink: Privately most feel their **job is safe**, and nothing much changes.
Their real worries are **money**, prices, bird flu, rent reviews and the owner **selling the farm**.
howTheyFeel: Most feel **calm** or mildly **uneasy**, with the same background money worry as now.
Those with thin savings feel **tired** and worn rather than afraid.

differences.text: Worry falls from 2.38 for farmers with thin savings to 1.14 for those with strong savings, and 40% of the thin group look for side income.
Adaptive farmers worry least (1.49 against 1.94 for resistant ones), and 73% of them keep learning AI tools while 99% of resistant farmers simply keep going.
Early-career farmers save most, at 53%, against 30% in mid-career, where worry is highest at 1.83.

quotes.name: Uma Petrov
quotes.text: If the Hallorans sell the farm, I lose my wages and my bed in the same week.

quotes.name: Beth Torres
quotes.text: If the computers stay stupid, my red calving notebook and I are safe on Hollins Farm for another twenty years.

quotes.name: Gareth Evans
quotes.text: Last year the AI spotted disease in the wheat four days before I'd have seen it walking the field.

thoughts.text: My job's safe and life carries on much as before.
Money stays tight: low pay, rent, loans and only weeks saved.
The farm could be sold, or the rent or grant could end.
Prices, weather and disease worry me more than any computer.
AI tools save me a bit of time, not money.

least.name: Farmers with savings
least.story: None has thin savings and most have strong ones, so they keep going and keep learning the tools; savings, not AI, set a farmer's peace of mind.

most.name: Weeks from the overdraft
most.story: Almost all have thin savings and most resist change; they cut spending and keep going, showing their fear is about money, not machines.

S1.headline: Most farmers expect office work to go first and see their hands-on work as safe for now, so they learn the tools and watch for robots.

whatTheyDo.text: About 49% learn the new tools, such as a pig-health record app or setting up AI box ordering themselves.
About 37% keep doing the stock work well, like lambing and sheep work, so the owner keeps them on.
About 33% bring in machines or software, for example pricing a shared egg grader or trialling a robot weeder.
About 28% act together, such as joining the farmworkers' union or pushing for written notice rules for farm housing.
About 28% save more, for example skipping the yearly weekend away or saving £60 a week instead of £40.

whatTheySay: Most say this is the **office's problem**: a cow still has to be fed by somebody.
Union members say workers need a **written deal** before new machines arrive.
whatTheyThink: Privately many think AI takes the **paperwork** they dislike, while **robots come slowly** to muddy farms.
Many fear a **robot milker** or feeder cutting their hours, or worry for a **partner's office job**.
howTheyFeel: Most feel **uneasy**, like hearing a noise in the yard at night.
Many feel more **worried for family** in office jobs than for themselves.

differences.text: Worry is 1.51 for adaptive farmers against 2.38 for resistant ones; 90% of adaptive farmers automate, while 73% of resistant ones just keep going.
Worry falls from 2.52 with thin savings to 1.69 with strong savings.
Progressive farmers turn to collective action far more, at 78%, than any other group.

quotes.name: Uma Petrov
quotes.text: A robot on the feed passage could cut my hours by a third, and a third of nothing much is a lot.

quotes.name: Adam Garcia
quotes.text: An AI that does my grain marketing at two in the morning is the best farmhand I've ever hired.

quotes.name: Carlos Ito
quotes.text: My girlfriend Mia checks mortgage applications at the bank, and that card reads like her job description.

thoughts.text: AI can take the paperwork I dislike, and that helps me.
My hands-on work is safe for years, because robots come slowly.
A robot or software could let the owner cut my hours or job.
My partner's or family's office job is more at risk than mine.
Big buyers, landlords and big farms would use AI to squeeze us.

least.name: The early adopters
least.story: Most adapt easily and few have thin savings; they automate and invest, treating AI as a farmhand, so knowing the tools is what protects these farmers.

most.name: Hands without a buffer
most.story: Most have thin savings and are slow to change; they save and learn the basics while eyeing robot feeders, so little cushion leaves farm workers exposed.

S2.headline: Almost every farmer is anxious or alarmed, expecting robots around 2031 to take their work, so most save, cut back and lean on family.

whatTheyDo.text: About 49% save every spare pound, for example cancelling a holiday or saving £250 a month as a fallback.
About 39% cut spending hard, such as selling the second car or cancelling the children's swimming lessons.
About 36% turn to family, like asking a parent about moving into the spare room.
About 34% turn to politics, signing petitions for a retraining plan or writing to their MP about farm robots.
About 26% change family plans, such as putting off children or shrinking the wedding.

whatTheySay: Most say it's **too fast** and the **government** must step in, slow it down or help.
Many say families, churches and **unions** will have to carry each other.
whatTheyThink: Privately most expect **robots around 2031** to take their job, with no other trade to fall back on.
Many fear losing a **second wage** in 2028, or **big robot farms** undercutting their prices.
howTheyFeel: Most feel **alarmed**: sick, sleepless, like the ground going soft underfoot.
Some feel **ashamed** at the thought of asking family for money.

differences.text: Worry is 3.85 for resistant farmers against 2.9 for adaptive ones; 70% of resistant farmers seek support, while 57% of adaptive ones automate.
Worry falls from 3.68 with thin savings to 3.12 with strong savings, and 52% of the thin group seek support.
78% of progressive farmers turn to politics, while traditional farmers lean more on support and family plans.

quotes.name: Yusuf Walsh
quotes.text: At 63 I'd lose the job and the cottage, four years before my pension. That's the whole thing, right there.

quotes.name: Beth Torres
quotes.text: Fourteen years I've been learning to spot a sick cow a day early, and a machine will learn the same trick in a week.

quotes.name: Tomas Baker
quotes.text: A firm with a thousand robots will always undercut a guy with two.

thoughts.text: Robots around 2031 will take my job, and I've no other trade.
Big robot farms will undercut our prices, and our farm won't pay.
My partner's or family's wage could go first, in 2028.
We could come through if we run the robots ourselves.
Owners or landlords will choose robots and sell or take back the land.

least.name: Owners who buy robots
least.story: Mostly late-career, adaptive and with strong savings, they invest in robots and bring family in; owning land and capital shields these farmers from fast change.

most.name: No plan B
most.story: Over half resist change and many have thin savings; they cut spending, lean on family and campaign, because they see no other work to move into.

S3.headline: With five years' warning, most farmers feel uneasy or anxious rather than alarmed, and use the time to save, retrain and plan.

whatTheyDo.text: About 56% save more, such as saving for a house deposit or paying down the land loan.
About 38% retrain, for example an evening course in farm machinery or a robot technician course.
About 30% invest, like putting money into a robot co-op with local farms or leasing a robot weeder.
About 30% change family plans, such as waiting to have children or steering a son towards engineering.
About 24% build side income, like charging small growers to set up AI planning.

whatTheySay: Most say there's **time**, so bosses and government should **plan it now**.
Many tell young people to **learn a trade** and not waste the five years.
whatTheyThink: Privately many think it's the **same ending, just later**, but with time to retrain or pay debts.
Older farmers think robots arrive about when they'd **stop anyway**.
howTheyFeel: Most feel **worried but steadier**, like a long winter they can see coming.
Some feel **guilty** about possibly wasting the time.

differences.text: Worry is 3.07 for resistant farmers against 1.91 for adaptive ones, and 60% of adaptive farmers invest.
Late-career farmers worry least, at 2.25 against 2.69 for early-career ones, and 65% of them save more.
Worry falls from 2.88 with thin savings to 2.2 with strong savings.
Traditional farmers lean on family plans most, at 58%.

quotes.name: Fatima Quinn
quotes.text: Two years would be a fire in the hen house, but five years is a long winter we can plan for.

quotes.name: Colin Kowalski
quotes.text: I'd tell my son that the safest job is the one where you're the person the machine calls when it's stuck.

quotes.name: Yusuf Walsh
quotes.text: The land agent would stop buying new heifers, run the herd down quiet, and let it go when I retire. No announcement.

thoughts.text: There's time to pay down loans and grow the farm before robots.
Robots come about when I'd stop anyway, so I nearly reach my pension.
Five years gives me time to retrain or learn to run robots.
It's the same ending, just later: I still lose the job.
My partner or children get time to change course too.
Prices, owners or the lease are still the bigger risk.

least.name: Owners near handover
least.story: Mostly late-career, adaptive and with strong savings, they invest in shared robots and hand farms to children, so time plus money lets farmers choose their machines.

most.name: Young and stuck
most.story: Nearly all early or mid-career and resistant to change, most with thin savings; they save, delay children and lean on unions, as extra years alone don't help.

S4.headline: Most farmers feel the robots are far enough off to carry on, and many expect to be retired or handing over by then.

whatTheyDo.text: About 69% keep working as now, like keeping 650 ewes and 40 suckler cows or milking at the same farm.
About 46% plan around family, such as buying a small house within ten years or handing the farm to a son.
About 32% save steadily, for example 150 a month towards a cushion or paying down a mortgage.
About 29% invest, like saving for a robot milker or putting money into a robot-sharing co-op.
About 19% retrain slowly, such as taking one college course each year.

whatTheySay: Most say ten years is **plenty of time**, so there's **no need to panic**.
Some say it leaves **no excuse** for not planning training and pensions.
whatTheyThink: Privately younger farmers think ten years is enough to **build a business** and own the robots.
Older farmers think they'll be **retired** first, and worry for their **children**.
howTheyFeel: Most feel **calm** or mildly **uneasy**, as it's a long way off.
The old **money worry** stays for those with thin savings.

differences.text: Worry is 2.36 for resistant farmers against 1.23 for adaptive ones, and 59% of adaptive farmers invest.
Worry falls from 2.23 with thin savings to 1.48 with strong savings.
91% of late-career farmers simply keep going, with worry of 1.65 against 1.96 in mid-career.
72% of traditional farmers plan around family, far more than other groups.

quotes.name: Adam Garcia
quotes.text: Ten years is long enough that the robots will be my son Mateo's tools, not my problem.

quotes.name: Zoe Lopez
quotes.text: Ten years feels like forever until it isn't.

quotes.name: Uma Petrov
quotes.text: If my boot splits or the car fails its test, my savings are gone, whether AGI comes in two years or ten.

thoughts.text: Ten years is enough to build my own business and own the robots.
I'll be retired or handing over before the robots arrive.
The old worries stay bigger: money, prices and who owns the farm.
By then the kids are grown and the mortgage nearly paid.
It's my children's and the young ones' world, not mine.
I'd still lose the job in the end, and might waste the decade.

least.name: Builders and retirees
least.story: Mostly adaptive with moderate or strong savings, they keep going, invest and plan family handovers; a decade's warning lets them turn robots into their own tools.

most.name: Slow to move
most.story: Most resist change and over half have thin savings; they keep going and save a little, so a decade's warning risks becoming a decade of waiting.
